children: Wall Street’s attention is split. Treasury yields have climbed across maturities as inflation worries resurface. At the same time, the 2-year/10-year
spread—the market’s most watched measure of curve slope—has compressed toward inversion.

That gap now stands near +19 basis points, still positive but the tightest reading since December 2024. The squeeze has been almost uninterrupted since December 2025. Roughly two years earlier, in late 2024, the same spread had just climbed back above zero after the long 2022–24 inversion.
The subsequent steepening never fully matured. Instead of rebuilding a durable premium for duration, the curve has flattened again as shorter-dated yields have kept pace with—or outrun—the long end.

A flattening curve with rising yields is a different signal from a flattening curve with falling yields. The former typically reflects firmer inflation expectations and a market that is repricing the path of policy higher, rather than pricing an imminent slowdown.

Investors are therefore watching two thresholds at once: whether the 10-year can hold its latest highs, and whether the 2s10s cushion of less than 20 basis points survives the next inflation print. A move back through zero would return the Treasury market to an inverted stance it left behind only two years ago.

title: Treasury curve flattens toward inversion amid fresh inflation jitters
